summary: Describes the algorithms that implement Boneh-Franklin and Boneh-Boyen identity-based encryption, in which a person's identity, such as an email address, serves as their public key. It is based partly on Voltage Security's IBCS documents. This is an informational memo.

plainLanguage.summary: Identity-based encryption (IBE) lets a sender calculate a recipient's public key from an identity and public information. A key server later checks the recipient and provides the matching private key. This document specifies two IBE algorithms and warns that it received limited IETF review.

questions: what is a private key generator
subtitle: How identity-based encryption uses a recipient's identity to derive a public key.

tldr.problem: In ordinary public-key encryption, a sender needs the recipient's public key before sending a protected message. RFC 5091 describes a system that can derive that public key from an identity string and shared public parameters.
tldr.mechanism: It specifies the Boneh-Franklin (BF) and Boneh-Boyen (BB1) encryption algorithms on type-1 supersingular elliptic curves. A Private-key Generator uses a master secret to issue the matching private key after authenticating the requester.
tldr.outcome: This Informational RFC gives implementation algorithms, but its IESG note says it received limited IETF review and asks readers to evaluate its value carefully. It has been updated by RFC 8996.

today: RFC 5091 is Informational and has been updated by RFC 8996. Its IESG note says it received limited IETF review and asks readers to evaluate it carefully.

sections.title: Identity-Based Encryption
sections.content:
RFC 5091 specifies two identity-based encryption (IBE) systems: Boneh-Franklin (BF) and Boneh-Boyen (BB1). In IBE, anyone with the system's public parameters can derive a public key from an identity string, such as a user identifier.

This avoids obtaining a randomly generated public key from the recipient before sending. IBE covers encryption only; a separate mechanism is needed for digital signatures. The IESG note says the document received limited review because of its specialized subject.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender uses a recipient's identity and public system information to calculate an encryption key. The RFC covers encryption, not digital signatures.

sections.title: The Public-Parameter Server and Key Generator
sections.content:
A complete IBE system has a Public Parameter Server (PPS) and a Private-key Generator (PKG). The PPS publishes shared public parameters and PKG policy information; the PKG keeps a master secret and uses it to create individual private keys.

A sender retrieves the recipient's public parameters from a known PPS location. The RFC requires the PPS location to be authenticated and says PPS and PKG servers must support TLS 1.1. A recipient authenticates to the PKG to obtain a private key, which must be sent over a secure connection.
sections.plainLanguage: The PPS provides public information that senders can retrieve. The PKG checks a user's identity before giving that user a private key.

sections.title: Encrypting and Reading a Message
sections.content:
To send a message, the sender chooses a content-encryption key (CEK), encrypts the message with it, and encrypts the CEK using the recipient's IBE public key. The recipient obtains the public parameters and the corresponding private key from the PKG, then uses the private key to recover the CEK and decrypt the message.

The PKG may authorize another party to obtain some private keys. The RFC gives a mail-filtering appliance as an example, because it could then decrypt and scan messages. How users authenticate to the PKG is central to the system's security.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender encrypts the message with a content key, then encrypts that key for the recipient's identity. The recipient gets a matching private key from the PKG and uses it to open the message key.

sections.title: The BF and BB1 Algorithms
sections.content:
Both algorithms use bilinear pairings on type-1 supersingular elliptic curves. The RFC limits this version to curves of the form y^2 = x^3 + 1, with prime p congruent to 11 modulo 12; other curve types are outside its scope.

BF derives the public key by hashing the identity onto the curve and produces a ciphertext tuple (U, V, W). BB1 has separate setup, key-extraction, encryption, and decryption procedures, and its ciphertext contains four values. Both encrypt a random symmetric session key rather than the whole message.
sections.plainLanguage: BF and BB1 use curve-based mathematics to connect an identity, public parameters, and a private key. They encrypt a random session key, which can then protect the message.

sections.title: Security and Key Control
sections.content:
The system depends on strong authentication before the PKG issues private keys, and on secure random values for the algorithms. The PKG and its administrators can create private keys for identities, so the RFC recommends controls and logging for administrators.

The RFC describes five security-strength levels and warns that the weaker key limits protection when IBE transports a stronger symmetric key. It also says identity formats must make hash collisions useless to an attacker. A short-lived identity component can support rekeying if a private key is compromised.
sections.plainLanguage: The PKG can create users' private keys, so access to its master secret needs careful control. Strong authentication and unpredictable random values are also necessary.
